title: Given a singly linked list L0 to L1 to ... to Ln, reorder it to L0 to Ln to L1 to Ln-1 to L2 to Ln-2 and so on. You may not change node values, only rearrange the nodes themselves.
shortTitle: Reorder List (L0 to Ln to L1 to Ln-1): Find Middle, Reverse, Merge
keyPoints: Split at the middle using fast-slow pointers, reverse the back half, then interleave front and back node by node.
The problem forbids changing node values, so physical relinking of nodes is required.
The interleave step must save each node's next before overwriting to avoid losing the chain.
For odd-length lists, the front half gets the extra node, and the merge terminates when the back half runs out.
The three-phase approach runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
This problem composes three well-known subroutines: find middle, reverse list, and alternating merge.

s1_definition.oneliner: Split at the middle, reverse the back half, then interleave front and back node by node.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Reorder pattern** – interleave a list with itself from both ends: first, last, second, second-last, and so on.
- **Phase 1** – find the middle with fast-slow pointers and split into front and back halves.
- **Phase 2** – reverse the back half in place.
- **Phase 3** – merge the two halves by alternating one node from front, one from reversed back.
- **Constraint** – node values cannot change; only node links may be rearranged.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, the risk team processes a queue of loan applications numbered 1 to n and wants to pair the earliest with the latest, then the second with the second-last. A clerk finds the middle of the queue, turns the back half around, then zips the two halves together: front, back, front, back.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
List: 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5

Phase 1: Find middle, split
  Front: 1 -> 2 -> 3
  Back:  4 -> 5

Phase 2: Reverse back half
  Back:  5 -> 4

Phase 3: Alternating merge
  first=1, second=5
  1 -> 5 -> 2      (first moves to 2, second moves to 4)
  2 -> 4 -> 3      (first moves to 3, second is null)
  Stop.

Result: 1 -> 5 -> 2 -> 4 -> 3
```

```text
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│         Reorder List Flow                     │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                              │
│   Phase 1: Find middle with fast/slow        │
│           Split into front + back            │
│              │                               │
│              ▼                               │
│   Phase 2: Reverse back half                 │
│              │                               │
│              ▼                               │
│   Phase 3: Alternating merge                 │
│   ┌──────────────────────────────┐           │
│   │ While back is not null:      │           │
│   │   save first.next, second.next│          │
│   │   first -> second -> firstNext│          │
│   │   advance both pointers      │           │
│   └──────────────────────────────┘           │
│                                              │
│   Result: L0 -> Ln -> L1 -> Ln-1 -> ...     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Reordering a linked list into the front-back interleaved pattern is a three-phase in-place algorithm. Find the middle and split, reverse the back half, then alternate one node from the front with one from the reversed back. The whole thing runs in O(n) time with O(1) space.

The merge phase is the trickiest part because you must save each node's next pointer before overwriting it. Losing the chain mid-merge is the most common bug.

At the National Bank of India, the risk team processed a daily queue of loan applications and wanted them reordered so each review pass paired the earliest with the latest. The queue was a singly linked list, and this three-phase algorithm produced the front-and-back interleaving in place.

The correctness detail is the split: by using `fast.next != null && fast.next.next != null`, the front half is never shorter than the back half, so the merge terminates cleanly on both odd and even lengths.

Remember one sentence: split at the middle, reverse the back half, and zip the two halves together node by node.
